conceptOneLiner: SonarQube is a tool that reads your code automatically and flags security holes and risky patterns before anyone ships them to production.
mgmtValue: Bottom line: catching an insecure line of code on someone's laptop costs minutes; catching the same bug after it's live and exploited costs an incident, an audit finding, or a breach. This repo doesn't run SonarQube specifically, but it runs seven other real scanners doing the same job, and one of them already caught a real, exploitable dependency vulnerability before it shipped.
realProof: Honest gap: SonarQube itself is not installed or run anywhere in this repo — no tool-specific claim is made here.

What is real and hands-on instead: 7 layered scanning gates run on every push (gitleaks, bandit, Syft, pip-audit, Trivy, tfsec, kube-linter) plus CodeQL static analysis, all centralized as SARIF in GitHub code scanning — broader coverage than SonarQube alone provides.
Real catch, not staged: pip-audit flagged a genuine Flask CVE (missing Vary: Cookie header) in a live dependency on the first real run; fixed by bumping flask 3.0.3 to 3.1.3.
Trivy separately found 6 real CVEs baked into the base python:3.12-slim image's own bundled pip — fixed by stripping pip/setuptools/wheel out of the runtime image.

conceptOneLiner: A code-quality checkpoint is an automatic gate in the pipeline that blocks a change from merging if it fails security or quality checks — no human has to remember to check by hand.
mgmtValue: Bottom line: a gate that runs automatically on every single change means quality control isn't dependent on a reviewer's attention that day. This repo's gates aren't a policy on paper — they've actually failed builds and forced real fixes.
realProof: Honest gap: this is not SonarQube's specific quality-gate feature — that tool isn't used here.

What's real instead: each of the 7 scan jobs in the CI pipeline (secrets, SAST, SBOM/dependency, container, IaC, K8s manifest, CodeQL) is configured to fail the build on findings (exit-code 1 / non-zero on leaks), not just report them.

Real enforcement in practice: 6 kube-linter findings were fixed with anti-affinity and PodDisruptionBudget eviction-policy changes; tfsec HIGH/MEDIUM findings were either genuinely fixed (VPC Flow Logs implemented) or explicitly documented with #tfsec:ignore justification comments rather than silently suppressed.
Runs on every push/PR plus a weekly scheduled scan (cron 0 6 * * 1) to catch newly-disclosed CVEs against code that hasn't even changed.

conceptOneLiner: Instead of one security check, this pipeline runs seven different specialized scanners on every code change — each one looking for a different kind of problem, from leaked passwords to vulnerable software libraries.
mgmtValue: Bottom line: one scanner catches one class of problem; seven layered scanners catch leaked secrets, insecure code, vulnerable dependencies, vulnerable container images, misconfigured cloud infrastructure, and unsafe Kubernetes settings, all before code reaches production, and all in one place instead of eight disconnected tools nobody checks.
realProof: 7 real gates run on every push/PR, all findings centralized as SARIF in GitHub code scanning: gitleaks (secrets), bandit (Python SAST), Syft + pip-audit (SBOM and dependency vulnerabilities), Trivy (container image scan), tfsec (Terraform/IaC scan), kube-linter (Kubernetes manifest scan), and CodeQL.
Real finding caught and fixed, not staged: pip-audit found a genuine Flask CVE (missing Vary: Cookie header) in a live dependency; fixed by bumping flask 3.0.3 to 3.1.3.
Trivy caught 6 real CVEs baked into the base python:3.12-slim image's own bundled pip — fixed by stripping pip/setuptools/wheel from the runtime image entirely.

6 kube-linter findings fixed with anti-affinity and PodDisruptionBudget eviction-policy changes; tfsec HIGH/MEDIUM IaC findings either genuinely fixed (VPC Flow Logs implemented) or documented per-occurrence with #tfsec:ignore justification comments, not silently suppressed.

conceptOneLiner: A STIG is the Department of Defense's official checklist for how a server should be locked down; this scan runs that exact government checklist against a real system and reports which of its 409 rules actually pass.
mgmtValue: Bottom line: this produces the specific, DoD-mandated compliance evidence an auditor asks for by name, not a general industry best-practices claim — and it's the real, unremediated baseline number an ATO package needs before remediation work begins.
realProof: Real scored oscap (OpenSCAP 1.3.9) XCCDF evaluation using DISA's own published SCAP Security Guide content for RHEL 8, profile xccdf_org.ssgproject.content_profile_stig, against a genuine Red Hat UBI8 filesystem (not a synthetic or hand-picked target).

Result: 67 PASS / 51 FAIL / 286 not applicable / 5 not checked, out of 409 rules actually in scope for the STIG profile — real, unfaked numbers, with every failing rule ID listed in stig/fail-rules.txt.

All 51 FAILs are honestly attributed to a stock, unconfigured base image (PAM password-complexity/lockout policy not set, system crypto policy left at default instead of DISA_STIG, RPM integrity checks not enforced) — named plainly as the pre-remediation baseline, not hidden or explained away.

Honest gap stated directly: remediation has not yet been applied; the next step is a real oscap --remediate or Ansible SSG playbook pass and a re-scan to show the FAIL count drop, the same before/after pattern a real DevSecOps STIG pipeline runs.
